solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Muslim leader has a cheek, breaking into church

indicators.note: to break into something is to get inside it

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for church
the article, kept as it is
lip is insolent talk, as in 'less of your lip'

explanation.surface: A religious leader behaves impudently by forcing his way into a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has a cheek' reads as one phrase about impudence, but 'has' only links and 'a cheek' is the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A caliph was the chief civil and religious ruler of the Islamic world, successor to Muhammad.

clue.text: From greasy spoon, a German stimulant

blocks.note: a greasy spoon is a cheap British café, informally a caff
the German for 'a' (feminine form)

explanation.surface: Someone gets their pick-me-up from a cheap diner, perhaps a German one.
explanation.walkthrough: A greasy spoon is a cheap, basic British café serving fried breakfasts; 'a German' asks for the German word for 'a', here EINE.
explanation.definitionFit: Caffeine is the compound in coffee and tea that acts on the nervous system to keep people alert.

clue.text: Religious reformer is very funny, and fat

blocks.note: text-speak for 'laugh out loud', said of something very funny
lard is pig fat

explanation.surface: A description of a preacher who is both hilarious and portly.
explanation.walkthrough: LOL is modern internet slang, an odd partner for a fourteenth-century movement.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lollards were followers of John Wycliffe in late medieval England, early critics of Church practice before the Reformation.

clue.text: Heath potentially made a first appearance

blocks.note: Edward Heath was British Prime Minister from 1970 to 1974
Heath's first name, Edward, in its short form
surface padding that flags this as just one way of describing the man

explanation.surface: A heathland perhaps turning up for the first time, or a politician debuting.
explanation.walkthrough: Heath looks like moorland, but it is Edward Heath, the British Prime Minister (premier) whose first name shortens to Ed; 'potentially' flags that this is only one way to describe him.
explanation.definitionFit: A play or film that premiered was given its opening public performance, its debut before audiences.

clue.text: Leaflet covering poor entertainment that kills the buzz

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for a thing, standing for the noun

indicators.note: a covering goes round what it covers

blocks.note: a flyer is a printed handbill
pap is worthless, mushy reading or viewing

explanation.surface: A pamphlet advertising a dull show that ruins everyone's good mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kills the buzz' reads as spoiling the fun, but the buzz is literal: flies buzzing.
explanation.definitionFit: Flypaper is sticky strip hung up to trap insects, which then die and stop their droning noise.

clue.text: Land cut back, one blocking airport that causes a glow in the dark

definitions.text: that causes a glow in the dark
definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for the thing, standing for the noun

blocks.note: to light on something is to land on it, as a bird lights on a branch
to lop is to cut off
Luton is an airport north of London
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A land-clearing and airport disruption that somehow leaves the night sky glowing.
explanation.walkthrough: Luton is one of London's airports; I is placed between its T and O.
explanation.definitionFit: Artificial illumination from towns scatters in the atmosphere and brightens the night sky, hiding stars.

clue.text: Call for truce heard in scout groups

indicators.note: what is heard is the sound of the word, not its spelling

blocks.note: pax is the British schoolchild's cry for a truce

explanation.surface: Squabbling young scouts hear someone call a ceasefire.
explanation.walkthrough: PAX, Latin for peace, was the playground word British children shouted to stop a fight.
explanation.definitionFit: Cub Scouts and Brownies are organised into units called packs, each led by adult volunteers.

clue.text: Bishop perhaps about to dip into church collection

indicators.note: dipping into something puts you inside it

blocks.note: the collection plate passed round in church
re means concerning

explanation.surface: A bishop is suspected of helping himself from the church's takings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' marks bishop as one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A prelate is a high-ranking cleric such as a bishop, archbishop or abbot.

clue.text: Do the dirty on some woman for preference

blocks.note: to rat is to betray or inform on someone
a pronoun for any woman

explanation.surface: Someone chooses to betray a particular woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do the dirty on' is one idiom in the surface, but the setter splits it, and 'on' only places the woman after the betrayal.
explanation.definitionFit: 'I would rather walk' expresses a preference, meaning more willingly or sooner.

clue.text: Remarkable rocky formation where unstable genius cast away

indicators.note: something unstable will not hold its shape, so the letters that follow move around

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 14 letters

explanation.surface: A striking rock outcrop where a troubled genius was marooned.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'cast away' a shipwrecked hermit; it is just fodder along with 'genius'.
explanation.definitionFit: This Northern Irish coast site has about forty thousand interlocking basalt columns, a famous natural wonder.

clue.text: Not confident, making changes by force

indicators.note: one thing by another sits beside it, so the two pieces are joined end to end

blocks.note: F is the physics symbol for force
to alter is to change

explanation.surface: Someone unsure of themselves pushes through reforms by strong-arm methods.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads 'making changes' first, but 'by force' puts F at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A faltering voice or step is hesitant and unsteady, lacking assurance.

clue.text: Fleece provides warmth, after cold

blocks.note: C for cold, as on a tap
heat is warmth

explanation.surface: A fleece jacket keeps you warm once you have come in from the cold.
explanation.walkthrough: Fleece looks like the jacket, but here it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To fleece someone is to swindle them out of money, as a sheep is stripped of wool.

clue.text: Transport uncle, for one, right away

blocks.note: an uncle is one kind of relative
R for right

explanation.surface: Someone arranges to ferry an uncle somewhere and get rid of him.
explanation.walkthrough: Transport looks like vehicles, but it is the old sense of being carried away by emotion.
explanation.definitionFit: Transports of joy are fits of rapture, so the word means great happiness or ecstasy.

clue.text: Seaport’s redevelopment not needed

indicators.note: redeveloping a place rebuilds it in a new arrangement, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

explanation.surface: Locals declare that the proposed rebuilding of the harbour town is unnecessary.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the phrase in 'time to spare', left over and surplus.
explanation.definitionFit: Something to spare is surplus, extra beyond requirements, so it is not required.

clue.text: Only partially clean a dirty bottom

indicators.note: only part of the words is used, so the answer lies inside a stretch of them

blocks.note: the last letter of 'clean', all of 'a', and the start of 'dirty'

explanation.surface: Advice on a half-hearted wash of a grubby backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottom' reads as a backside in the surface, but it is the lowest point.
explanation.definitionFit: A nadir is the lowest point of anything, the opposite of a zenith.

clue.text: Disreputable, in without a date, drooped

indicators.note: the first word goes in the second, so it sits inside the abbreviation

blocks.note: louche means shady, of doubtful morals
s.d. is the bibliographic abbreviation for sine die or 'no date'

explanation.surface: A shady character without a partner for the evening sagged in disappointment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without a date' suggests being dateless; it is s.d., the abbreviation used in catalogues for a book printed without a date.
explanation.definitionFit: To slouch is to sit or stand with a lazy, drooping posture.

clue.text: School briefly allowed to be partnered in immoral activity

blocks.note: short for comprehensive, a British state secondary school
licit means lawful or permitted

explanation.surface: A school permitted to join in some shady business.
explanation.walkthrough: A comprehensive is the standard British state secondary school, taking pupils of all abilities.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone complicit is involved with others as an accomplice in wrongdoing.

clue.text: Three Sisters run being cancelled in venues bearing fine

blocks.note: places where plays are staged
R for run, from cricket scoring
F for fine, as on pencil leads

explanation.surface: A production of Chekhov's Three Sisters is cancelled in theatres that face a penalty.
explanation.walkthrough: Three Sisters suggests the Chekhov play, whose surface fits the theatres, but the sisters are the three goddesses of Greek myth.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek mythology the three Moirai spun, measured and cut the thread of every human life.

clue.text: Pass on social occasion for sport

indicators.note: one thing on another is placed next to it, joining the two words

blocks.note: to hand something is to pass it
a ball is a formal dance party

explanation.surface: Someone declines a party invitation because of a sports fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass on' looks like one phrase meaning decline; the setter splits it.
explanation.definitionFit: Handball is a team game where players throw a ball into the opposing goal.

clue.text: Select a beer, taking work over

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned over means read upwards

blocks.note: the article, kept as it is
a pint of beer
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: Someone chooses a beer and takes over the job.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversed opus goes between the P and INT of the beer.
explanation.definitionFit: To appoint someone is to choose them for a post or role.

clue.text: Lawn in front covered in a lot of fertiliser

indicators.note: the front of the word for grass is its opening letter
a covered thing is inside its cover

blocks.note: much means a great deal
the opening letter of lawn

explanation.surface: A gardener heaps manure over the front lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'a lot of fertiliser' as one phrase, but 'a lot of' is the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Mulch is decaying organic matter spread on soil, which enriches it and feeds plants.

clue.text: One spotted curtain length turned up, concealing nothing

indicators.note: concealing something means holding it inside
in a down clue, turned up means read from bottom to top

blocks.note: a drape is a curtain
O looks like zero
L for length

explanation.surface: A curtain was hemmed up but hid nothing, and someone noticed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One spotted' reads as a person who was seen; it is an animal with spots.
explanation.definitionFit: The leopard is the big cat famous for its rosette-patterned coat, as in 'a leopard can't change its spots'.

clue.text: Textile is wonderful, almost sumptuous

indicators.note: almost means not quite all

blocks.note: fab is slang for fabulous
rich loses its final letter

explanation.surface: A shopper admires a cloth as marvellous and nearly luxurious.
explanation.walkthrough: Rich is cut short to RIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Fabric is woven or knitted cloth, the material garments and furnishings are made from.

clue.text: A large tree next to small plants

indicators.note: being next to means sitting alongside, so the pieces join in a row

blocks.note: the article, kept as it is
L for large, as on clothing
a pine is a conifer
S for small, as on clothing

explanation.surface: A big tree growing beside some little plants in a garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small plants' looks like one phrase, but 'small' is S and 'plants' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Alpines are low-growing flowers native to high mountains, popular in rock gardens.

clue.text: Nosy, first to look a veteran nursing home over

indicators.note: the first of the next word is its opening letter
in a down clue, over turns the whole string to read upwards

blocks.note: the opening letter of look
the article, kept as it is
san is short for sanatorium, a home for nursing the sick, here one for old soldiers

explanation.surface: An inquisitive person looks first at a retired soldier's care home.
explanation.walkthrough: Nosy looks like prying, but here it is the literal sense, to do with the nose.
explanation.definitionFit: Nasal describes anything relating to the nose, such as a nasal passage or spray.

clue.text: Informed about female with flea in ear?

blocks.note: to be informed is to be told
of can mean concerning, as in 'tales of adventure'
F for female

explanation.surface: Someone is warned about a woman who has an insect in her ear.
explanation.walkthrough: To send someone off with a flea in their ear is a British idiom for scolding them sharply; the question mark flags the idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone sent away with a flea in their ear has been sharply rebuked, which is being scolded.

clue.text: Engineers text covering one cathedral

definitions.note: Reims is the city famous for its cathedral

blocks.note: the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
MS is a manuscript
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Engineers producing a written report about a cathedral they restored.
explanation.walkthrough: RE, the Royal Engineers, is the British army corps of engineers; Reims stands for its cathedral, where French kings were crowned.
explanation.definitionFit: Reims in northern France is known for its Gothic cathedral, coronation site of French monarchs.

clue.text: Scouting technique’s thrown a crowd of townsmen at first

indicators.note: something thrown is scattered, so the letters land in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters
the opening letter of townsmen

explanation.surface: A scouting skill is on display, but townspeople crowd around and throw it off.
explanation.walkthrough: The townsman's first letter joins the fodder before it is mixed.
explanation.definitionFit: Woodcraft is the skill of living and finding one's way in the forest, central to the scouting movement.

clue.text: Farm animals always knocked over orchid

indicators.note: something knocked over ends up upside down

blocks.note: cows and bulls
ay (or aye) is an old word for ever

explanation.surface: Farm cows keep trampling a delicate flower.
explanation.walkthrough: AY meaning always is archaic, familiar mainly from poetry and 'for ever and ay'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cattleya is a genus of large showy tropical orchids from the Americas, popular as corsages.

clue.text: A demon barber and son quarrelling

blocks.note: the article, kept as it is
Sweeney Todd, the Demon Barber of Fleet Street
S for son, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: A murderous barber and his son are arguing.
explanation.walkthrough: Sweeney Todd is the murderous barber of Victorian melodrama and Sondheim's musical.
explanation.definitionFit: People at odds are in disagreement or conflict, which is arguing.
